mainTopic: לשון הרע and the מצורע, the מצוה of תוכחה and its limits, not switching lodgings or crafts, and the smallest amount of יסורין.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an answer: one item atones for לשון הרע said in secret, and another for לשון הרע said in public. Two teachings then explain why a מצורע sits alone and brings birds, since both match his sin of splitting people apart with chatter. A ברייתא on 'לא תשנא את אחיך בלבבך' teaches that hidden hatred is forbidden and that one must rebuke a friend, even many times, but never to the point of shaming him. Sages lament how few people can take rebuke or give it well, and רבי יוחנן בן נורי tells how רבי עקיבא loved him more for his criticism. The גמרא then rules that ענוה, even שלא לשמה, beats תוכחה לשמה, and illustrates this with רב הונא and חייא בר רב. Next come three views on how far rebuke must go, all learned from שאול and יהונתן, followed by rules about not switching one's lodging or one's family craft. The amud ends by defining the smallest amount of יסורין and explaining why it matters: someone who goes forty days with no suffering has already received his reward. A teaching from ארץ ישראל begins at the very end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the answer: the other one atones for public speech
steps.stepSummary: The last words of an earlier answer. One item atones for לשון הרע said in secret, and the other atones for לשון הרע said in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: And that one is for speech said in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began just before this line. Two different things atone for לשון הרע, and this line says the second one covers לשון הרע spoken in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, two sources seemed to say that two different things atone for the same sin of לשון הרע. The answer is that they are not the same case. One covers speech in secret, and this line says the other covers speech in public.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This one... that one': a way of answering a contradiction by showing that each source is talking about a different case

phrases.english: That one is for speech in public.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the 'this one... that one' answer from the earlier part of the sugya.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (secret speech vs. public speech)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two items seemed to atone for the very same sin.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each item atones for a different kind of לשון הרע: one for secret speech, one for public speech.

steps.title: Why must the מצורע sit alone?
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נדב asks why the תורה makes a מצורע live alone, outside the camp. There are different versions of whom he asked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נדב asked רבי חנינא. Some say it was רבי שמואל בר נדב, the son-in-law of רבי חנינא, who asked רבי חנינא. Some say he asked רבי יהושע בן לוי. He asked: What is special about a מצורע, that the תורה says 'he shall sit alone; outside the camp shall be his dwelling'?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins: why is the punishment of a מצורע to be sent away and live alone? The גמרא also gives different versions of who asked whom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other people who are טמא are not made to sit completely alone the way a מצורע is. So the question is what makes the מצורע different. The question expects an answer that matches his sin, and the answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a question put to a teacher)
A person struck with צרעת, a skin affliction

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נָדָב מֵרַבִּי חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nadav asked Rabbi Ḥanina,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נָדָב
phrases.english: and some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Nadav,
the son-in-law of Rabbi Ḥanina, who asked Rabbi Ḥanina,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ מֵרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: and some say he asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi:
What is different about a leper, that the Torah said
"He shall sit alone; outside the camp shall be his dwelling"?
phrases.notes: ויקרא 13:46

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נָדָב מֵרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of what atones for לשון הרע to the reasons behind the punishment of the מצורע.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the מצורע in particular must be sent out to live alone.

steps.title: He separated people, so he is separated
steps.stepSummary: The answer: with his לשון הרע the מצורע separated husband from wife and friend from friend. So the תורה separates him from everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: He separated between a man and his wife, and between a man and his friend. Therefore the תורה said, 'He shall sit alone...'
steps.whatsHappening: This answers the question from the last step. The punishment fits the sin: the person who pulled people apart is now set apart himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לשון הרע breaks up relationships, whether between husband and wife or between friends. The תורה punishes him with the same thing he did: he caused loneliness, so he is made to sit alone. This is the idea of מידה כנגד מידה.
steps.whatToRemember: The מצורע sits alone because his לשון הרע split people apart. The punishment matches the sin.

phrases.english: He separated between a man and his wife,
between a man and his friend;
therefore the Torah said: "He shall sit alone, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Measure for measure: he separated others with his speech, so he is separated from everyone.

steps.title: Why the מצורע brings birds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן לוי explains why the מצורע brings two birds for his purification. He chattered, so he brings birds, which chatter all the time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן לוי said: What is special about a מצורע, that the תורה said he must bring two birds for his purification? הקדוש ברוך הוא said: He did an act of chatter, so the תורה said he should bring an offering of chatter.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching explains another rule of the מצורע, the birds he brings to become טהור. Here too the tool he uses for his טהרה fits his sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Birds chirp and chatter all the time. The מצורע sinned by talking too much in a harmful way. So his טהרה uses birds, which reminds him of his chatter. Together with the previous teaching, this shows that every part of the מצורע's process is connected to לשון הרע.

keyTerms.meaning: Two birds, used in the טהרה of the מצורע
The Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.whatToRemember: The birds stand for chatter: the מצורע chattered, so he brings birds that chatter.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Levi said:
What is different about a leper, that the Torah said
he must bring two birds for his purification?
phrases.notes: ויקרא 14:4

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
He did an act of chatter,
phrases.notes: The chatter he means is the לשון הרע the מצורע spoke.

phrases.aramaic: לְפִיכָךְ אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה יָבִיא קׇרְבַּן פַּטִּיט.
phrases.english: therefore the Torah said he must bring an offering of chatter.
phrases.notes: Birds chirp all the time, so they are the 'chatter' offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן לֵוִי: מָה נִשְׁתַּנָּה מְצוֹרָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'מה נשתנה' pattern to explain a second rule of the מצורע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The birds of the מצורע match his sin of chattering לשון הרע.

steps.title: Does 'do not hate' mean do not hit or curse?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes 'לא תשנא את אחיך בלבבך' and considers a possible reading: maybe the פסוק only forbids acting on hatred by hitting, slapping or cursing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'Do not hate your brother in your heart.' One might think it means: do not hit him, do not slap him, and do not curse him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins with a ברייתא. The ברייתא suggests a possible reading of the פסוק so that it can reject it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'יכול' brings in a mistaken idea: that 'do not hate' only forbids showing hatred through actions. The ברייתא raises this idea only to explain why the פסוק adds the word 'in your heart'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One might think': brings in a reading that will be rejected

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"You shall not hate your brother in your heart"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:17

phrases.english: one might think: he may not hit him, may not slap him,
and may not curse him?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא תִשְׂנָא אֶת אָחִיךָ בִּלְבָבֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא about hatred between people. It connects to the topic of how people treat each other.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the prohibition of hating is only about outward acts of hatred.

steps.title: 'In your heart': the פסוק means hidden hatred
steps.stepSummary: The word 'בלבבך' shows that the פסוק is talking about hatred kept inside the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'in your heart': it is talking about hatred in the heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question. The extra word 'in your heart' shows the פסוק forbids even hatred that is never shown on the outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the word 'בלבבך' we might have thought only acts of hatred are forbidden. The פסוק adds 'in your heart' to teach that hidden hatred, which no one sees, is itself forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The פסוק teaches us to say': brings in the proof from the words of the פסוק
Hatred in the heart, hidden hatred

steps.whatToRemember: 'לא תשנא את אחיך בלבבך' forbids hidden hatred in the heart, not only outward acts of hatred.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean hitting or cursing is allowed. It only means that this particular פסוק is about the hatred inside, which is forbidden even when it is never shown.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "in your heart";
the verse is speaking of hatred in the heart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'יכול' reading from step 5 by pointing to the word 'בלבבך'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'בלבבך' shows the prohibition is about hidden hatred in the heart.
steps.whyThisMatters: It establishes that the תורה forbids a feeling, not only an action. Hidden hatred is itself an איסור.

steps.title: Where does the duty to rebuke come from?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks for the source that someone who sees a friend doing something wrong must rebuke him.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that if you see your friend doing something improper, you must rebuke him?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a new question: where does the תורה say we must correct a friend who does wrong? It is setting up the next step, where it will bring a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the ברייתא spoke about hatred hidden in the heart. Now it moves to the next part of the same פסוק and asks for the source of the duty of תוכחה.

keyTerms.meaning: From where (do we know)? A request for a source
To rebuke him, to correct him

phrases.english: From where do we know that one who sees in his friend
an improper thing
that he is obligated to rebuke him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first half of the פסוק (hatred) to the next half (rebuke)
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the obligation of תוכחה

steps.title: The source is the פסוק 'הוכח תוכיח'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'הוכח תוכיח' commands us to rebuke.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'You shall surely rebuke.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with the words 'הוכח תוכיח'. The תורה directly commands us to correct our friend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These words come right after 'לא תשנא את אחיך בלבבך' in the same פסוק. So instead of keeping hatred inside, a person should speak up and correct the friend.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely rebuke (the word is said twice)

phrases.english: As it is stated: 'You shall surely rebuke.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:17

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'הוכח תוכיח' is the source

steps.title: What if he did not listen the first time?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how we know you must rebuke again if the friend did not accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he rebuked him and the friend did not accept it, from where do we know he must rebuke him again?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a follow-up question: is one try enough, or must you try again? It is setting up a teaching from the doubled word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think that once you have rebuked, you have done your job. The question checks whether the מצוה goes further than one attempt.

keyTerms.meaning: That he should go back and rebuke him again

phrases.english: If he rebuked him and he did not accept it,
from where do we know that he must go back and rebuke him again?

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹכִיחוֹ וְלֹא קִבֵּל מִנַּיִן שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר וְיוֹכִיחֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the basic obligation to a repeated case
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one must repeat a rebuke that was not accepted

steps.title: The doubled word means: rebuke again and again
steps.stepSummary: The extra word 'תוכיח' teaches that you must rebuke in any case, even many times.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'תוכיח' (an extra time), meaning: in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא learns from the doubled word 'הוכח תוכיח' that you must keep rebuking. One try is not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה could have said the word once. Saying it twice teaches that the מצוה continues even after the first attempt fails.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, no matter what

phrases.english: The verse says: 'You shall rebuke,'
phrases.notes: This is the second, extra word of 'הוכח תוכיח'. The doubling is what teaches us to repeat.

phrases.english: in any case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled verb teaches that one must rebuke repeatedly

steps.title: Even if it embarrasses him?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא considers whether you must keep rebuking even when the friend's face changes from shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think you must continue even if his face changes color from embarrassment.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא suggests a possible reading: since you must rebuke 'in any case', maybe that includes embarrassing him. It is setting up a limit that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מכל מקום' sounds like there is no limit at all. The ברייתא tests whether even public shame is allowed, so that it can then set a boundary.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought (a possible but wrong idea)
His face changes color, meaning he is shamed

phrases.english: One might think: even if his face changes?
phrases.notes: A changing face means he turns pale or red from shame.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limit of 'מכל מקום' from step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the obligation extends to rebuke that humiliates

steps.title: Never embarrass him: 'לא תשא עליו חטא'
steps.stepSummary: The end of the פסוק forbids sinning through the rebuke, so you may not shame him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Do not bear sin because of him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers with the end of the same פסוק. You may not commit a sin, embarrassing him, while you rebuke him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The duty to rebuke is strong, but it has a clear limit. Once the rebuke causes shame, the person rebuking becomes the one who is sinning.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not bear sin because of him

steps.whatToRemember: תוכחה: (1) it is a מצוה to rebuke, (2) you must repeat it if he does not listen, (3) you must never embarrass him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the הלכה framework for תוכחה: it is required and repeated, but it ends where shaming begins.

phrases.english: The verse says:
'Do not bear sin because of him.'
phrases.notes: The end of the same פסוק, ויקרא 19:17.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר לֹא תִשָּׂא עָלָיו חֵטְא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the possible reading of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Rebuke may not reach the point of humiliation

steps.title: רבי טרפון: hardly anyone can accept rebuke
steps.stepSummary: רבי טרפון doubts anyone in his generation accepts תוכחה, because people answer back by pointing out the rebuker's bigger faults.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי טרפון said: I wonder if anyone in this generation accepts rebuke. If you tell him 'remove the splinter from between your eyes', he answers 'remove the beam from between your eyes.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא: רבי טרפון complains that people do not accept correction. Instead they attack the one correcting them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'splinter' is a small fault and a 'beam' is a huge one. The person being rebuked turns it around: 'You have much bigger problems than I do!'

keyTerms.meaning: I wonder, I would be surprised
A splinter, a small chip of wood

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Tarfon said:
I would be surprised
if there is anyone in this generation
who accepts rebuke,
for even if he says to him
'Remove the splinter from between your eyes,'
he answers him
'Remove the beam from between your eyes.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּמֵיהַנִי אֲנִי אִם יֵשׁ בַּדּוֹר הַזֶּה שֶׁמְּקַבֵּל תּוֹכֵחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the laws of תוכחה, describes the practical difficulty of receiving it
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People of this generation do not accept rebuke; they deflect by pointing out the rebuker's larger faults

steps.title: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה: hardly anyone knows how to rebuke
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה doubts anyone knows how to rebuke properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה said: I wonder if anyone in this generation knows how to rebuke.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה looks at the other side: the problem is the people giving rebuke. They do not know how to do it properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי טרפון blamed the listener, and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה blames the speaker. This ties back to step 12: correct rebuke must not embarrass.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said:
I would be surprised if there is anyone in this generation
who knows how to rebuke.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּמֵיהַנִי אִם יֵשׁ בְּדוֹר הַזֶּה שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ לְהוֹכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel statement: shifts the difficulty from the receiver to the giver
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Few people know how to give rebuke correctly

steps.title: רבי יוחנן בן נורי: rebuking עקיבא made him love me more
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן בן נורי often complained about רבי עקיבא, who was punished for it, yet עקיבא loved him even more, fulfilling 'הוכח לחכם ויאהבך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן בן נורי said: I call heaven and earth as witnesses that עקיבא was punished many times because of me, since I complained about him to רבן שמעון. Yet I only made him love me more. This fulfills the פסוק: 'Do not rebuke a scoffer or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן בן נורי gives a real example of someone who accepted correction well: רבי עקיבא. The more he was criticized, the more he loved the one criticizing him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After two statements that rebuke rarely works, this story shows when it does: a חכם is glad to be corrected. That is exactly what the פסוק in משלי says.

keyTerms.meaning: I call heaven and earth as witnesses (a strong oath-like statement)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said:
I call upon heaven and earth as my witnesses
that many times
Akiva was punished because of me,
because I would complain about him
before Rabban Shimon the Great,
and all the more I added love in him (for me),
to fulfill what is stated:
'Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you;
rebuke a wise man and he will love you.'
phrases.notes: משלי 9:8

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעִיד אֲנִי עָלַי שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ שֶׁהַרְבֵּה פְּעָמִים לָקָה עֲקִיבָא עַל יְדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a positive counter-example: a חכם who received rebuke with love
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wise person responds to rebuke with greater love, as משלי 9:8 says

steps.title: Which is better: pure rebuke or impure humility?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה son of רבי שמעון asks which is better: תוכחה done for the right reason, or ענוה done for the wrong reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה, son of רבי שמעון, asked him: rebuke for its own sake, and humility not for its own sake — which of them is better?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question compares two good traits. One is speaking up with a pure motive, and the other is keeping quiet humbly but with an impure motive. It sets up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes a person must choose between speaking up and staying humble and quiet. The question asks whether a pure motive (לשמה) outweighs the type of trait itself.

keyTerms.meaning: For its own sake, with a pure motive
Not for its own sake, with another motive

phrases.english: He asked of him,
phrases.notes: He is asking his father, רבי שמעון.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon:
Rebuke for its own sake
and humility not for its own sake,
which of them is better?

steps.triggerLanguage: תּוֹכֵחָה לִשְׁמָהּ וַעֲנָוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ הֵי מִינַּיְיהוּ עֲדִיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of תוכחה by weighing it against ענוה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether pure rebuke outranks impure humility

steps.title: Agreed: pure humility is the greatest
steps.stepSummary: The father first gets his son to agree that ענוה לשמה is better, since ענוה is greatest of all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Don't you agree that humility for its own sake is better, as the Master said: humility is greater than all of them?
steps.whatsHappening: The father starts his answer with something both of them agree on: pure ענוה beats everything. This sets up the next move, which goes further.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He sets down a shared starting point. ענוה לשמה clearly wins, because ענוה is the top trait. Now he only needs to show that even ענוה שלא לשמה still wins.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Don't you agree that humility for its own sake is better,
as the Master said:
humility is greater than all of them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering step 16 by setting an agreed premise
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Pure ענוה is certainly better, since ענוה is the greatest trait

steps.title: Even impure humility is better, since impure leads to pure
steps.stepSummary: Even ענוה שלא לשמה is better, because רב teaches that doing good for the wrong reason leads to doing it for the right reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: Not for its own sake is also better, as רב יהודה said in the name of רב: a person should always study תורה and do מצוות even not for their own sake, because from 'not for its own sake' he comes to 'for its own sake.'
steps.whatsHappening: The father gives his final answer: ענוה wins even with an impure motive. He proves it from רב's famous teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Impure ענוה is not stuck at its low level, because it will grow into pure ענוה. Since pure ענוה is the greatest trait, the impure kind already carries that value and beats תוכחה לשמה.

keyTerms.meaning: A person should always occupy himself

steps.whatToRemember: ענוה is the greatest trait. Even ענוה with an impure motive beats pure תוכחה, because 'מתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה'.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not say an impure motive is ideal. It says the impure deed is worth doing because it leads to the pure one.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב's teaching 'מתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה' is a basic principle about motivation in learning and מצוות, quoted throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: Not for its own sake is also better,
as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
A person should always engage
in Torah and מצוות
even if not for their own sake,
because through doing it not for its own sake
he comes to do it for its own sake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the agreed premise of step 17 to impure humility, completing the answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ענוה, even שלא לשמה, is preferable to תוכחה לשמה, because שלא לשמה leads to לשמה

steps.title: What do these two ideas look like in real life?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a practical example of תוכחה לשמה and ענוה שלא לשמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does rebuke done for the right reason look like, and what does humility done for the wrong reason look like?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just compared these two things in the previous step. Now it asks for a real example of each, and it is setting up a story as the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 16-18 talked about these ideas in the abstract. This question asks for a concrete picture, so the learner can see how both can show up in one event.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it look like? What is the case?
Rebuke done for its own sake, for the right reason
Humility done not for its own sake, for some other reason

phrases.english: What is considered rebuke for its own sake
and humility not for its own sake?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a concrete example of the two ideas compared in steps 16-18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real-life case showing תוכחה לשמה and ענוה שלא לשמה.

steps.title: The story of רב הונא and חייא בר רב before שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא stopped bothering חייא בר רב when asked. He told שמואל his side of the story only in private, so that the son of רב would not be embarrassed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא and חייא בר רב were sitting before שמואל. חייא בר רב said: 'Look, master, he is bothering me.' רב הונא agreed not to bother him anymore. After חייא left, רב הונא told שמואל: 'He did such and such to me.' שמואל asked: 'Why didn't you say it to his face?' רב הונא answered: 'Heaven forbid that the son of רב should be embarrassed because of me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a story. רב הונא had a real complaint against חייא בר רב, but he kept quiet in front of him and only explained himself after חייא left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's tough treatment of חייא was a rebuke with a real reason behind it, which makes it תוכחה לשמה. His backing down was not true forgiveness or humility. He did it so as not to shame the son of his teacher רב, so it was ענוה שלא לשמה. Even so, it was still a good act, which fits רב's rule from step 18.

keyTerms.meaning: He took upon himself, he agreed
To his face, in his presence

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא וְחִיָּיא בַּר רַב
phrases.english: Like this incident with Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav
who were sitting before Shmuel.
Chiyya bar Rav said to him:
See, master, that he is distressing me.
phrases.notes: "He" is רב הונא, who was sitting right there.

phrases.aramaic: קַבֵּיל עֲלֵיהּ דְּתוּ לָא מְצַעַר לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He accepted upon himself that he would no longer distress him.
After he left, he said to him:
phrases.notes: After חייא בר רב left, רב הונא spoke to שמואל.

phrases.english: He did such and such.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי לָא אֲמַרְתְּ לֵיהּ בְּאַנְפֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why didn't you say it to his face?
He said to him: Heaven forbid for me
that the offspring of Rav should be embarrassed through me!

steps.whatToRemember: One act can be both: the rebuke had a real and proper reason, while the backing down came from respect for רב rather than pure humility.
steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא וְחִיָּיא בַּר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19 with a story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The incident of רב הונא, who rebuked for a real reason but backed down only to avoid shaming רב's son.

steps.title: How far does the duty to rebuke go?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new question: up to what point must a person keep rebuking someone?
steps.simpleTranslation: Until what point must one keep rebuking?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic about the limits of rebuke. It is setting up a disagreement among the אמוראים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה of rebuke has a limit at some point. The question is what reaction from the other person ends the obligation.

phrases.english: Until where does rebuke extend?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the quality of rebuke to its limits.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The point at which the obligation to rebuke ends.

steps.title: Three views: hitting, cursing, or scolding
steps.stepSummary: רב says until hitting, שמואל says until cursing, and רבי יוחנן says until an angry scolding.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: until he hits you. שמואל says: until he curses you. רבי יוחנן says: until he scolds you angrily.
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים give three different limits for rebuke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each view names a different reaction from the person being rebuked. רב requires the most patience, because you keep going until he actually hits you. רבי יוחנן lets you stop earliest, as soon as he angrily scolds you.
steps.confusionAlert: The hitting, cursing or scolding is done BY the person being rebuked, AGAINST the one rebuking him. It is not the rebuker who hits!

phrases.english: Rav says: Until hitting;
and Shmuel says: Until cursing;
and Rabbi Yochanan says: Until reprimand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 with three opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Until hitting (רב), until cursing (שמואל), until reprimand (רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: The same argument among the תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The same three-way argument already appears among רבי אליעזר, רבי יהושע and בן עזאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like a disagreement of the תנאים: רבי אליעזר says until hitting, רבי יהושע says until cursing, בן עזאי says until scolding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that this exact argument already existed in the earlier generation of the תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each אמורא's view is now backed by a תנא: רב matches רבי אליעזר, שמואל matches רבי יהושע, and רבי יוחנן matches בן עזאי. So none of the three views is new or alone.

keyTerms.meaning: Like a disagreement among the תנאים

phrases.english: It is like a dispute of tanna'im:
Rabbi Eliezer says: Until hitting;
Rabbi Yehoshua says: Until cursing;
ben Azzai says: Until reprimand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the אמוראים' argument in step 22 matches an earlier argument among תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three-way argument about the limit of rebuke goes back to the תנאים.

steps.title: All three learned from one story about שאול and יהונתן
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says that all three views come from the פסוקים about שאול getting angry at יהונתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: All three learned from one passage: 'שאול grew angry at יהונתן and said to him: you son of a rebellious woman,' and it is written: 'שאול threw the spear at him to strike him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק shows that all three opinions share one source: the story where יהונתן stood up for דוד and his father שאול reacted harshly. He is setting up how each view reads it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יהונתן had in effect rebuked his father. שאול's reaction went in stages: anger, insulting words, and finally throwing a spear. Each opinion will pick a different stage as the limit.

keyTerms.meaning: They learned from one passage in the פסוקים
Son of a rebellious, crooked woman (an insult)

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
And all three of them expounded one verse:
"And Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan,
phrases.notes: שמואל א 20:30

phrases.english: and he said to him: You son of perverse rebellion";
and it is written: "And Saul cast the spear
phrases.notes: שמואל א 20:33

phrases.english: at him to strike him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a shared scriptural source for the three views in steps 22-23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All three opinions are drawn from the story of שאול's reaction to יהונתן.

steps.title: Matching each view to its words in the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: Hitting comes from 'to strike him', cursing comes from 'to the shame of your mother's nakedness', and scolding comes from 'שאול's anger was kindled'.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the one who says until hitting: it is written 'to strike him.' For the one who says until cursing: it is written 'to your shame and the shame of your mother's nakedness.' For the one who says until scolding: it is written 'שאול's anger was kindled.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows which words in the story each opinion relies on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יהונתן kept speaking to his father through each stage of the story. Each opinion holds that the obligation to rebuke lasts until the stage it points to: the anger, the cursing words, or the spear.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
Your mother's nakedness (part of שאול's insult)

steps.whatToRemember: The limit of rebuke is argued three ways (hitting, cursing, scolding), and all three views come from different stages of שאול's reaction to יהונתן.

phrases.english: According to the one who says: Until hitting,
it is because it is written: "To strike him";
and according to the one who says: Until cursing,
it is because it is written: "To your shame and to the shame of your mother's nakedness";
phrases.notes: These words come later in the same פסוק, שמואל א 20:30.

phrases.english: and according to the one who says: Until reprimand,
it is because it is written: "And Saul's anger was kindled."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out how each opinion reads the פסוקים quoted in step 24.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Each opinion about the limit of rebuke is tied to a different stage of שאול's reaction: anger, cursing, or striking.

steps.title: Challenge to the view of 'until scolding'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: according to the one who says rebuke continues only until scolding, the פסוק also mentions hitting and cursing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to the one who says you rebuke only until scolding: the פסוק also writes hitting and cursing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's view that a person must rebuke only until he gets scolded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 25 each opinion was tied to a different part of the story of שאול and יהונתן. But יהונתן's story did not stop at scolding. He was also cursed and nearly struck, and he kept on speaking up anyway. So why should the rule stop at scolding?

phrases.english: And according to the one who says: until scolding,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוחנן from step 22.

phrases.english: but hitting and cursing are written!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר נְזִיפָה, הָכְתִיב הַכָּאָה וּקְלָלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks one of the three readings of the פסוק given in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion that rebuke is required only until scolding (נזיפה).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source story itself shows יהונתן continuing past scolding, into cursing and hitting, so the limit should be higher.

steps.title: יהונתן went beyond the requirement out of love for דוד
steps.stepSummary: יהונתן's case was special: he loved דוד so much that he put himself through more than the law requires.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there. Because יהונתן loved דוד so much, he put himself through more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that יהונתן took extra abuse only because of his great love for דוד, not because the הלכה required it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer separates what יהונתן actually did from what the law demands. The obligation itself ends at scolding. יהונתן's willingness to be cursed and almost hit was his own extra step, so it does not set the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Gave himself over, put himself at risk

steps.whatToRemember: All three views (hitting, cursing, scolding) come from the שאול–יהונתן story. The view of scolding explains that יהונתן went past the requirement only because he loved דוד.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because, on account of the extra fondness
that Jonathan had for David,
he gave himself over more.
phrases.notes: He means יהונתן took more than he had to. It was his choice, not the law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the source shows extra devotion, not the basic obligation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story proves that a person must keep rebuking even past cursing and hitting.
steps.terutzMaskana: יהונתן's case was beyond the requirement because of his love for דוד. The obligation itself ends at scolding.

steps.title: How much must a guest bear before changing lodging?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: up to what point should a person not move out of his lodging place?
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to what point should a person not change his lodging place?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new, related question about how much bad treatment a guest must put up with before he moves to a different host.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the theme of putting up with someone else's anger. The question assumes there is a basic rule that a guest should not switch lodgings, and it asks where that rule stops.

keyTerms.meaning: Lodging place, inn, the host's home

phrases.english: Up to what point should a person not change
his lodging place?

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד הֵיכָן לֹא יְשַׁנֶּה אָדָם בָּאַכְסַנְיָא שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'עד היכן' format as step 21 to start a related topic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The limit of mistreatment a guest must accept before he may change lodgings.

steps.title: רב: until hitting; שמואל: until he is thrown out
steps.stepSummary: רב says a guest stays until he is hit. שמואל says until his belongings are thrown over his back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: until hitting. שמואל says: until they throw his belongings over his back.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give their answers: רב sets the limit at hitting, and שמואל sets it at being thrown out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance שמואל seems to demand more patience, since being thrown out goes further than being hit. The next step will show that the real argument is narrower than it looks.

keyTerms.meaning: His belongings onto his back, meaning he is being sent away

phrases.english: Rav says: until hitting,
and Shmuel says:
until they throw his belongings over his back.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: עַד הַכָּאָה, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: until the guest is hit. שמואל: until his belongings are thrown over his back.

steps.title: They argue only when the host hits his wife
steps.stepSummary: Both agree that a guest may leave if he himself is hit or if he is thrown out. They argue only when the host hits his own wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the host hits the guest himself, everyone agrees he may leave. If the host throws his belongings over his back, everyone also agrees. Where they argue is when the host hits his wife. One master holds: since the host does not hurt the guest himself, what difference does it make to him? The other master holds: the guest will end up being drawn into a fight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the argument between רב and שמואל. Both cases mentioned are agreed on, and the real dispute is about a host who hits his wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This changes how we read step 29. Since both agree that a guest who is hit himself may leave, רב's 'until hitting' must mean the host hitting his wife. So רב lets the guest leave at that point, because staying will drag him into a fight. שמואל, whose limit is being thrown out, says the guest stays, because the host is not hurting him.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees, there is no argument
What difference does it make to him?
He will come to be drawn into a fight

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רב's 'until hitting' as the host hitting the guest, because both agree the guest may leave then. רב's 'hitting' means the host hitting his wife, and at that point רב lets the guest leave.

phrases.english: When the host hits him himself
phrases.notes: Here 'him' means the guest.

phrases.english: everyone agrees,
when his belongings are thrown over his back
everyone also agrees,
where they argue
is when the host hits his wife.
One master holds:
phrases.notes: This first 'master' is שמואל, who says the guest stays.

phrases.english: since he does not hurt the guest himself,
what difference does it make to him?
And the other master holds: he will come to be drawn into a fight.
phrases.notes: This is רב, who lets the guest leave once the host hits his wife.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּהַכָּאָה דִּידֵיהּ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains exactly which case רב and שמואל argue about in step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both agree a guest may leave if he is hit or thrown out. When the host hits his wife, רב says he may leave and שמואל says the guest stays.

steps.title: Why is staying put so important?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a guest must put up with so much rather than simply move.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why all this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the rule that a guest should not switch lodgings easily. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 28–30 asked a guest to bear a lot of unpleasantness. Here the גמרא asks what the point of all that patience is.

phrases.english: And why all this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the rule discussed in steps 28–30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason a guest must endure so much before changing lodgings.

steps.title: A guest who moves hurts himself and his host
steps.stepSummary: Because a guest who switches lodgings harms both his host's reputation and his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the master said: a guest damages and is damaged.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that moving out hurts the good name of both the host and the guest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a guest leaves, people assume something went wrong. Either the host was unpleasant or the guest was hard to live with. So staying protects everyone's reputation, and that is why the guest should put up with a lot first.

keyTerms.meaning: Damages and is damaged; hurts others' reputation and his own

steps.whatToRemember: A guest should not change his lodging lightly. Both agree he may leave if he is hit or thrown out. When the host hits his wife, רב says leave and שמואל says stay. The reason is that moving harms the reputation of both host and guest.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a lasting lesson in דרך ארץ: how we act as guests reflects on our hosts, so we should be patient before walking away.

phrases.english: As the master said:
A guest damages and is damaged.
phrases.notes: If he moves, people will think badly of the host and of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A guest who changes lodgings harms both his host's reputation and his own.

steps.title: רב's Torah source for not switching lodgings
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב brings a Torah source that a person should not change his lodging place: אברהם returned 'to the place where his tent had been at the beginning.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Where in the Torah do we see that a person should not change his lodging place? It says: 'to the place where his tent had been at the beginning.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a Torah source for the idea from the previous steps: a person should not switch his lodging place. רב points to אברהם, who went back to the same places he had stayed before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the reason was practical: switching lodgings hurts the host's reputation and your own. Now רב shows the same behavior in the Torah. When אברהם came back from מצרים, the פסוק stresses that he returned to the exact spot where his tent had been before. The word 'tent' suggests a real, settled place to stay.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
From where do we know that a person should not change
his lodging place, from the Torah?
As it says: 'To the place where there was'
'his tent at the beginning.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 13:3. This is about אברהם coming back from מצרים to the same spots he stayed on the way down.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא יְשַׁנֶּה אָדָם בָּאַכְסַנְיָא שֶׁלּוֹ מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a Torah source to the practical reason given in step 32 for not switching lodgings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should not change his lodging place. The source is אברהם returning 'to the place where his tent had been at the beginning.'

steps.title: A different source from the same verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא learns the same lesson from an earlier phrase in the פסוק: 'and he went on his journeys.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: We learn it from here: 'And he went on his journeys.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second sage agrees with the lesson but points to a different phrase in the same פסוק. He learns it from 'and he went on his journeys,' meaning the same stops אברהם made on the way down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sages agree that you should not switch lodgings. They only disagree about which words teach it. The phrase 'his journeys' is about stops along a trip, not a settled home. That difference sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: And he went on his journeys, meaning the same stops as before

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
From here: 'And he went on his journeys.'
phrases.notes: These are earlier words in the same פסוק, בראשית 13:3.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא אָמַר מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source within the same פסוק for the lesson רב taught.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The source for not switching lodgings is 'and he went on his journeys.'

steps.title: What difference do the two sources make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether there is any practical difference between the two sources.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the two sources lead to any different result in real life. This short question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both sources teach the same rule, why does it matter which one we use? The גמרא assumes that a different source should mean some different result. It asks us to find it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them? A request for the practical difference between two opinions.

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical difference between the sources in steps 33 and 34.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether there is a practical difference between learning the rule from 'his tent' and learning it from 'his journeys.'

steps.title: The difference: a passing, temporary lodging
steps.stepSummary: The difference is a temporary lodging used only while passing through.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is a temporary lodging.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sources differ about a place you stay in only briefly, while passing through on a trip.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's word 'tent' suggests a settled, more permanent place. So by his source, the rule may apply only to a regular lodging. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's word 'journeys' is about stops on the road. So by his source, even a brief stopover should not be switched.

keyTerms.meaning: A temporary lodging, used only now and then or while passing through

steps.whatToRemember: Both sages agree that you should not switch lodgings. רב's source ('his tent') points to a settled lodging. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's source ('his journeys') covers even a short stop on the road.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them:
a temporary lodging.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They differ about a temporary lodging. 'Journeys' includes it, while 'his tent' points to a settled lodging.

steps.title: Don't leave your craft or your fathers' craft
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that a person should not leave his own craft or his fathers' craft. He proves it from חירם, the coppersmith who came to work for שלמה המלך.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Where do we see that a person should not change from his craft or from his fathers' craft? It says: 'And King שלמה sent and took חירם from צור. He was the son of a widow from the tribe of נפתלי, and his father was a man of צור, a worker in copper.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a related lesson in the same style ('don't switch'). This time the topic is work: stay with your craft and your family's craft. רבי יוחנן shows that חירם did the same copper work as his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is set up just like the lodging lesson, with the question 'מנין שלא ישנה אדם.' The פסוק stresses that חירם's father was a copper worker, and חירם himself was brought to do copper work. So he kept his father's trade. The next step shows that the same craft also ran in his mother's family.

keyTerms.meaning: His fathers, his family's earlier generations
A worker or craftsman in copper or brass

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
From where do we know that a person should not change from his craft
and from the craft of his fathers?
As it says: 'And King Solomon sent'
'and took Hiram from Tyre.'
phrases.notes: מלכים א 7:13–14. The next פסוק says חירם did all the copper work for שלמה.

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה הוּא מִמַּטֵּה נַפְתָּלִי
phrases.english: 'He was the son of a widow, from the tribe of Naphtali,'
'and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in copper.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא יְשַׁנֶּה אָדָם מֵאוּמָּנוּתוֹ וּמֵאוּמָּנוּת אֲבוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, related teaching in the same 'don't switch' pattern as step 33, now about one's craft.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should not leave his own craft or his fathers' craft. חירם did the same copper work as his father.

steps.title: Hiram's mother came from Dan, Oholiab's tribe of craftsmen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that חירם's mother was from the tribe of דן. That is the tribe of אהליאב, the master craftsman of the משכן. So חירם continued the craft of his mother's family too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Master said: His mother was from the house of דן. And it is written: 'And with him was אהליאב, son of אחיסמך, of the tribe of דן.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי יוחנן's proof. It shows that חירם's craft also ran in his mother's family, since she came from דן, the tribe of the craftsman אהליאב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A known teaching ('אמר מר') places חירם's mother in the house of דן. The Torah describes אהליאב of the tribe of דן as one of the skilled builders of the משכן. So skilled craftsmanship ran in that family. חירם kept up the craft of his ancestors on both sides, which strengthens the lesson of step 37.

keyTerms.meaning: The house, or tribe, of דן
אהליאב, one of the master craftsmen who built the משכן

steps.confusionAlert: Step 37's פסוק says חירם's mother was from נפתלי, but here she is 'from the house of דן.' This comes from a different פסוק (דברי הימים ב 2:13), and the גמרא simply accepts it as known. Don't get stuck on the mismatch. The point here is only that her family was from דן, the tribe of skilled craftsmen.
steps.whatToRemember: Just as a guest should not switch lodgings, a person should not leave his family's craft. חירם kept the craft of his father and of his mother's tribe, דן, the tribe of אהליאב.

phrases.english: And the Master said:
His mother was from the house of Dan,
phrases.notes: Based on דברי הימים ב 2:13, which calls חירם 'the son of a woman of the daughters of דן.'

phrases.english: and it is written: 'And with him was Oholiab,'
'son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.'
phrases.notes: שמות 38:23. אהליאב helped build the משכן, so this shows דן was a tribe of skilled craftsmen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יוחנן's proof by showing the craft also came from חירם's mother's tribe.
steps.raayaObject: That חירם continued the craft of his ancestors (his fathers' craft) on his mother's side as well.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching that חירם's mother was from דן, together with שמות 38:23, which names אהליאב of the tribe of דן as a craftsman of the משכן.

steps.title: What is the smallest amount of suffering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how small a hardship can be and still count as יסורין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to what point is the limit of suffering?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question: what is the very least that still counts as suffering? It is setting up a list of answers that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not about great pain. It is about the lowest edge of the category: what tiny annoyance still counts as יסורין?

phrases.english: Up to where is the limit of suffering?
phrases.notes: He means: what is the smallest thing that still counts as suffering?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of חירם and keeping one's craft.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The minimum hardship that still counts as יסורין.

steps.title: A garment that doesn't fit
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the minimum is having a garment woven for you that doesn't fit right.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: anyone for whom they wove a garment to wear, and it does not fit him well.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives the first answer. A garment made especially for you that doesn't fit counts as suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a small disappointment. You expected something made for you, and it didn't work out. רבי אלעזר places the lowest level of יסורין here.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not suit or fit him

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
Anyone for whom they wove a garment to wear
and it does not fit him well.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: כׇּל שֶׁאָרְגוּ לוֹ בֶּגֶד לִלְבּוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 39.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An ill-fitting garment made for you is the minimum suffering.

steps.title: Even smaller things count: wine mixed at the wrong temperature
steps.stepSummary: רבא זעירא objects that the חכמים already said even smaller annoyances count, like hot and cold water mixed up in one's wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא זעירא, and some say רבי שמואל בר נחמני, objected: They said even more than this. Even if they meant to mix his wine with hot water and mixed it with cold, or meant cold and mixed it with hot, it counts. And you say all this?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא זעירא challenges רבי אלעזר. The חכמים counted something even smaller as suffering, so why set the bar as high as a whole garment?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is that רבי אלעזר's example is too big. If getting your drink at the wrong temperature already counts, then a ruined garment is far above the minimum.

phrases.english: Rava the Younger objected to this,
and some say it was Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani:
They said even more than this:
Even if they intended to mix his wine with hot water
and they mixed it for him with cold;
or with cold, and they mixed it for him with hot,
and you say all this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אלעזר's answer as setting the bar too high.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's garment example as the minimum.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים already counted a smaller annoyance (wrong water temperature) as suffering, so the garment cannot be the minimum.

steps.title: Even a shirt put on the wrong way
steps.stepSummary: מר בריה דרבינא says even a garment that comes out turned the wrong way counts as suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בריה דרבינא says: even if his shirt turned over on him.
steps.whatsHappening: Another sage lowers the bar even further. Putting on your shirt and finding it backward or inside out also counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the suffering is only the small bother of taking the shirt off and putting it on again. The list keeps getting smaller.

phrases.english: Mar son of Ravina said:
Even if his shirt turned over on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבִינָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ נֶהְפַּךְ לוֹ חֲלוּקוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an even smaller example of suffering.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A shirt put on the wrong way counts as suffering.

steps.title: Reaching for three coins and pulling out two
steps.stepSummary: Several sages, or a ברייתא, say even reaching into your pocket for three coins and coming up with two counts as suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא, and some say רב חסדא, and some say רבי יצחק, and some say it was taught in a ברייתא: even if he reached into his pocket to take three coins and two came up in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The smallest example yet: you reach for three coins and only get two, so you have to reach in again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bother here is only a second reach into the pocket. Even this tiny extra effort counts as יסורין.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא; a teaching from the time of the משנה

phrases.english: Rava said, and some say it was Rav Chisda,
and some say it was Rabbi Yitzchak,
and some say it was taught in a baraita:
Even if he reached his hand into his pocket
to take three coins, and two came up in his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ הוֹשִׁיט יָדוֹ לַכִּיס לִיטּוֹל שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the smallest example in the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coming up short when taking coins from your pocket counts as suffering.

steps.title: Only when you get fewer coins, not more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא clarifies that it counts only when you get too few coins. Getting too many is no bother, because you can just drop the extra one back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Specifically three, and two came up in his hand. But two, and three came up in his hand, no, because there is no effort in throwing it back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the coin case. Getting fewer coins than you wanted counts as suffering, but getting more does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule depends on effort. Pulling out too few means reaching in again, which is a real bother. Pulling out too many takes almost no effort to fix, so it is not suffering.
steps.whatToRemember: Even the tiniest bother, like reaching into your pocket a second time, counts as יסורין. A mistake that is effortless to fix does not.

phrases.english: Specifically when he wanted three and two came up in his hand,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שְׁתַּיִם וְעָלוּ בְּיָדוֹ שָׁלֹשׁ — לָא,
phrases.english: but if he wanted two and three came up in his hand, no,
because there is no effort in throwing the extra one back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the coin case from step 43 to coming up short.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only coming up short counts, because only that takes extra effort.

steps.title: Why does all this matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it is so important to define the smallest amount of suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why all this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we needed this whole list of tiny sufferings. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Defining the lowest level of suffering seems like an odd thing to spend time on. The גמרא wants to show there is a real reason behind it.

phrases.english: And why all this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the purpose behind the whole list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why it matters to know the minimum amount of suffering.

steps.title: Forty days without suffering
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught that anyone who goes forty days with no suffering has already received his reward. Then the גמרא begins to bring what they say in ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: anyone who goes forty days without suffering has received his world. In the West they say:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the list matters. Going forty days with no suffering at all is a bad sign, so it is good to know that even tiny bothers count. The last words introduce a teaching from ארץ ישראל that continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some suffering is seen as good, because it means a person's reward is being saved for עולם הבא. A person with no suffering at all may be getting his whole reward now. Since tiny annoyances count, most people do not fall into that worrying group.

keyTerms.meaning: The school (study house) of רבי ישמעאל
He has received his world, meaning his reward
In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the whole list. Because even small bothers count as יסורין, the worrying case of forty days with no suffering at all is very rare.
steps.confusionAlert: "Received his world" does not mean he received עולם הבא. It means he got his reward here, in this world.

phrases.english: As the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Anyone who has had forty days pass over him
without suffering has received his world.
phrases.notes: He has already gotten his reward in this world, so less is left for עולם הבא.

phrases.english: In the West they say:
phrases.notes: "The West" is ארץ ישראל. Their teaching continues in the next lines of the גמרא.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל: כֹּל שֶׁעָבְרוּ עָלָיו אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 45, then opens a teaching from ארץ ישראל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Forty days with no suffering means a person has received his reward in this world, so it matters to know what counts as suffering.
